subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN
speechtext:
On August 28, 1958, Mr. Speaker, my colleague the Minister of Finance reported to the house on a special meeting that had been held in Washington under the auspices of the international bank to consider means of alleviating India's foreign exchange difficulties. The Minister of Finance stated at the time that in the light of that meeting it appeared that the most helpful thing Canada can do is to continue to provide India with the Canadian goods she may require in her development program.
In the intervening months there have been detailed discussions between Canadian and Indian officials as to the type of assistance that would be most effective in helping India carry forward her economic development program and which Canada was in the best position to provide. I am pleased to be able to inform the house today that as a result of these discussions it has been agreed that $17 million will be made available to India out of the Colombo plan appropriation for the fiscal year 1958-59 to enable the Indian government to purchase in Canada essential commodities and equipment which they have requested from us.
Of the $17 million, $1 million will be applied to the Canada-India reactor to enable the work on that project to go forward; $10.5 million will be devoted to the provision of industrial raw materials including aluminum, copper and nickel, which are urgently needed by India in various phases of her development program and which will help sustain adequate levels of industrial activity and employment; $2.5 million will be provided in the form of railway sleepers-which I interpret as railway ties-to assist in the expansion and improvement of railway facilities in India; $2.5 million will be made available in the form of fertilizers which are required in connection with India's program to increase her food production; $120,000 will be devoted to the purchase of another three Cobalt beam therapy units for use in Indian hospitals. Discussions covering allocation of the balance of the funds
being made available to India in the current fiscal year are still in progress.
In all cases where Canadian aid is taking the form of commodities, the Indian government has agreed to establish local counterpart funds equivalent to the amount of the Canadian grant. These counterpart funds, as in the past, will be used to cover the local costs of economic development projects agreed upon by our two governments.
The house will be aware, Mr. Speaker, that over the past 15 months Canada was also able to assist India in meeting her requirements of food grains by making available a total of $48 million in the form of grants and loans for the purchase of Canadian wheat. Of this amount $7 million has been provided under the Colombo plan and $41 million over and above the assistance available to India under the Colombo plan.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of the house will welcome the statement the minister has just made with regard to the assistance which is to be provided to India under the Colombo plan. I understand from his statement that from the appropriation of $50 million which the government intends to ask from parliament, $17 million will be used for assistance to India. I am glad that the minister has emphasized the desirability-I think he emphasized it-of giving this assistance in the form which was originally contemplated under the Colombo plan, that is capital assistance, and that the amount of $7 million for wheat that was made available last year for India, to which he referred, is not to be taken as a normal practice under the Colombo plan. I think the minister will agree that it was the intent of the Colombo plan that the assistance given should be capital and technical and not in the form of consumer goods, except when there was an emergency and when the country concerned, because of that emergency, desired that form of assistance.

subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the announcement that has been made this morning. We of the C.C.F. recognize, as I am sure other members of the house do, that India is the bastion of freedom in Asia and that with her second five-year plan she has experienced some rather serious difficulty. I am sure the Canadian people will welcome any assistance to India to help her develop her economy.

Our position with regard to economic assistance is clear. We believe that the government should have set aside a much larger sum of money than has been done on any previous occasion in order to provide for economic assistance to undeveloped countries generally. We feel that the main purpose of the Colombo plan has been capital and technical assistance. We have always said that whenever it became necessary, from India's point of view, to use part of these funds in an emergency for the purchase of food, we were quite in agreement that that be done. We feel the two things generally should be kept separate, namely the Colombo plan for capital assistance and economic development and the other necessary measures taken to assist India to meet her difficult problem of feeding the people of that nation.

subtopic: WHEAT-STATEMENT ON CHANGE IN PRICING POLICY

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: WHEAT-STATEMENT ON CHANGE IN PRICING POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an announcement to make with regard to the Canadian wheat board pricing policy. Due to the fact that with the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway the largest lake vessels will be able to carry wheat directly from the lakehead to St. Lawrence ports, with a consequent saving in transportation costs, the Canadian wheat board has introduced a change in its pricing policy.
The board announced that effective January 30, 1959, there would be an increase in the lakehead price of wheat of 5f cents per bushel, exclusive of a J cent exchange adjustment in price due to a decline in the premium on the Canadian dollar that day. As wheat is usually purchased by the buyers, and ocean freight arranged several weeks ahead of the intended date of shipment, the Canadian wheat board found it necessary to announce these changes in selling prices at this time, even though the seaway will not be open to navigation until late April of this year.
This increase, which represented the board's preliminary estimate of the gross saving in freight likely to be realized, was put into
[Mr. Argued

effect to ensure that the benefits of the seaway would be reflected in an increase in the final payment to western producers.
The increase applies only to the board's lakehead prices. Other than the daily exchange variation to which they are subject, no change was made in the board's selling prices for wheat for shipment from St. Lawrence, Atlantic and Pacific coast ports, or from Port Churchill.
The laid-down prices of wheat in the United Kingdom, European and other markets from these ports have not been affected by the increase in lakehead prices.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister a question. As a consequence of the minister's statement, or the announcement which he has made, does it not follow that there will be a reduction of 5 to 6 cents per bushel on wheat, as announced several years ago by the former government?

subtopic: WHEAT-STATEMENT ON CHANGE IN PRICING POLICY
speechtext: A reduction of what?

subtopic: WHEAT-STATEMENT ON CHANGE IN PRICING POLICY

subtopic: WHEAT-STATEMENT ON CHANGE IN PRICING POLICY
speechtext: Will the minister allow the hon. member for Assiniboia to comment on his statement before replying?

subtopic: WHEAT-STATEMENT ON CHANGE IN PRICING POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the increase which took place in the price of wheat at Fort William and Port Arthur a week ago today, according to press reports at that time of 51 cents a bushel-the minister says today 5f cents a bushel-was a very important one. This will result in an increased return to western grain producers on almost one-half the total wheat crop that is marketed from the three prairie provinces. This is a dividend that the prairie region is receiving, or will receive, from the St. Lawrence seaway. When I first saw the announcement in the press stemming from Winnipeg I wondered if the government's footwork in parliament was not just a little clumsy, because I had expected that this very important announcement would be made here perhaps simultaneously with the change at Fort William and Port Arthur. Nevertheless, it is a very important announcement.
I may have misunderstood the statement of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), but I think the action taken in this case by the Canadian wheat board was the right one, namely that the advantage

should accrue to the western grain producers while maintaining the principle that they have followed now for a few years of selling the grain at lakehead ports and the Pacific coast at the same price. This, Mr. Speaker, I calculate, based on recent history, should result in a one-year period in an increase in income to the grain producers of western Canada of something between $7 million and $8 million.
This is a very important step which has been taken. I express the hope now that other action with regard to wheat will not take away any substantial part of this advantage. As a matter of fact, some part of this increase has already been lost by a change in demurrage charges, and I hope there will be no increase in handling charges of grain in the future to detract from this very important step that the Canadian wheat board has now taken.

subtopic: WHEAT-STATEMENT ON CHANGE IN PRICING POLICY
speechtext:
In answer to the question of the hon. member for Laurier, this is a reflection of the reduced transportation charges which will come about as a result of the opening of the seaway, and the western producer will get the benefit of that reduction in transportation charges. It will not necessarily be to the full amount of 5| cents. It might be somewhat under that; nevertheless it will be substantial.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: DR. ROUSSEAU-STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON PRESS REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I have seen the statement that is reported in the press as having been made by Dr. Rousseau. If the statement was made as quoted in the press it is inaccurate. I do not intend to deal with the inaccuracies in detail;
I do not think any purpose would be served thereby. There are, however, two points that I should like to make very clear.
Dr. Rousseau is quoted in the press report as having said:
Notwithstanding the statement attributed by the newspapers to Hon. Alvin Hamilton, Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the Department of Agriculture has never offered me any position whatsoever.
Fortunately for the truth, Mr. Speaker, the offer of the position to Dr. Rousseau was made by my deputy minister in the presence of two witnesses, including a representative of the professional institute of the public service of Canada. It was also made in a letter dated January 20 from my deputy minister to Dr. Rousseau. The offer was a firm offer and was for 30 days. In view of the fact that a member of the civil service has taken this procedure of making a statement to the press, I am going to take the liberty of quoting from a letter from my deputy minister to Dr. Rousseau written on January 20, to which letter I have already referred. I am prepared to table the letter. The relevant portion is on page 3, and reads as follows:
As I told you on December 15, the Department of Agriculture have available a senior scientific position in the field of botany that is available for you should you wish to accept it. It may be that there are other positions outside the public service that you would prefer to take. If not, I would strongly urge that you consider the position in the Department of Agriculture most seriously. It is purely scientific and would, I am sure, provide new opportunities of service in a field in which you are eminently qualified.
The minister is quite prepared that you should have 30 days from today in which to consider this matter. If you do not choose to accept the position in the Department of Agriculture or any other that you think preferable I would appreciate it if you would submit your resignation at the end of 30 days. If you have not taken action in one way or the other during that time the minister will be faced with the unfortunate necessity of recommending your separation from the public service of Canada.
As I said in my statement the other day, the civil service commission of Canada has

been kept informed of all negotiations with Dr. Rousseau. The second point with which I should like to deal is found in this statement by Dr. Rousseau in the newspaper report:
Notwithstanding the repeated requests I made to the minister's secretary for an interview with Mr. Hamilton, and in spite of the assurance given to me that the minister would take no decision whatsoever without having the opportunity to discuss the matter with me, no interview was ever granted.
The facts are that I told my deputy minister many weeks in advance of his interviews with Dr. Rousseau, and also instructed my private secretary who was present at the interview of January 20, to tell Dr. Rousseau that if he so requested I was available at any time to see him. Dr. Rousseau has at no time asked to see me either directly or through my deputy minister or through my personal office. The assurance was given to Dr. Rousseau that all the known relevant facts would be weighed by the minister before arriving at a decision. This, Mr. Speaker, has been done.

speechtext: I should like to make it clear to the hon. member and to the house, as I have to the poultry producers associations for the past several months, that the decline in the price of broiler chickens, which is the biggest item, is due almost entirely to the very large increase in production which has taken place in Canada. 699. Prairie Farm Assistance Act administration- further amount required, $225,000.
Would the minister give an explanation for this particular vote?

The necessity for this vote arises, Mr. Chairman, from the fact that this year there was widespread drought throughout the prairie provinces and as a result a very large number of applications for inspections throughout the townships across the entire west. The estimate for administrative costs of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is made each year on the basis of the average cost in years past, particularly in the immediately past years. If you have a heavy inspection program as a result of adverse weather conditions it means that your administrative costs are considerably greater than the amount estimated.
This was the case in this particular year. A great many more inspections had to be made and there was a great deal more travelling to be done than had been the case in the two or three years previous. This amount of money is required to cover the costs of these extra inspections and the travelling expenses of the inspectors.

I am pleased to support this vote. I have often said in the past, and I repeat, that I think the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been of great benefit to western Canada. I believe that over the years this act has been amended from time to time in such a way as to generally improve its administration and the benefits provided under the act, and to make it at least somewhat more certain that farmers who in fact suffer crop failure are able to obtain payments.
Before the amendments were introduced into this act during the last session I had a very large number of complaints about its administration and the difficulty of getting payments. I want to tell the minister, in fairness, that the amendments made last year have reduced the number of complaints very substantially. I think the amendments have been in the right direction. The minister
[Mr. Robichaud.l
will recall that over the years when he and I sat almost together on this side of the house, both the Conservative party and the C.C.F. party put forward the idea that in so far as practicable payments should be made on an individual basis so that when a farmer has a crop failure he obtains payment. This objective has not been reached, and it may be a very long time before it is reached. Certainly, however, with one or two exceptions some years ago about which we had many long and heated arguments, the general direction has been to make it easier for farmers to qualify.
I should like, in just a very few sentences, to say that I think the government should consider an expansion of this act. It is not something new that I say today, but something I have been saying for some considerable length of time. I feel that in relation to the purchasing power of the dollar and in relation to the cost of farming, it is very essential that the benefits under this act be increased. We have had arguments in this house on other occasions about several matters.
I am not going to refer to that matter in such a way as to be ruled out of order. However, we have had arguments to the effect that certain other action, namely the $1 an acre payment, was being taken on that basis in order to make certain that farmers who had marketed little grain in past years would receive at least that minimum benefit as compared to what might be received if the deficiency program had been adopted.
I suggest that this is the kind of measure, Mr. Chairman, that should be used and should be expanded in order to make certain that farmers who have a crop failure receive the benefits that come from the national treasury. If it is the general purpose of the government, in supplementing agricultural income, to do so in such a way as to help the small farmers, the farmers who have been unfortunate enough to have crop failures, then this is the act that is designed to do that very thing and it is not designed to be done in some other act to that extent.
I should like to see the benefits under this act increased, as I said last session, to at least $10 per acre from the maximum of $4 per acre. Ten dollars per acre, if paid on the same basis as at present, is not a fabulous sum of money in relation to the cost of doing business and in relation to the cost of farming. One of the first reports I studied when I came to this house in 1945 was a submission which was made by the late R. E. Motherwell on the whole question of prairie farm assistance and the whole field of crop insurance. While many studies have been made since

that time I nevertheless believe that from the studies made by Mr. Motherwell during that time one can learn a great deal as to the problems that are involved in a prairie farm assistance scheme and those that may be involved in a crop insurance scheme. There may be some areas of Canada and some crops to which crop insurance is particularly adaptable. A crop insurance scheme perhaps has a different meaning to different people. But if a crop insurance scheme should attempt to be actuarially sound on the basis that each farmer and each farm shall pay into the scheme over a long period of years enough money to cover all of the benefits that are paid out, on that basis the crop insurance plan will be too expensive for the people who need it most. In the high risk areas the premiums would be exorbitant. I want to say that in the working out of any crop insurance plan-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is out of order, Mr. Chairman.

I will not wait, Mr. Chairman, until you rise. I will attempt to keep my remarks confined to this subject. As I said initially, there are in this plan some important features that I think should be retained in any plan that is adopted by parliament. One of them is universal coverage, where everyone is covered in this huge area and everyone has a chance to benefit if he has a crop failure. Another thing I like about prairie farm assistance is that under the act universal payments are made by all agricultural producers. Another feature of prairie farm assistance that has always appealed to me is the fact that it is a federal plan affecting three provinces. It does not say, generally speaking, to agricultural producers within one province as compared to those in another, "You have had more crop failures than other areas; therefore it will be necessary for you to pay more," or in other words that they should attempt to lift themselves by their own boot straps. I am saying to the minister that any scheme that is brought forward either to supplement or to replace the act-and I do not think there is any suggestion from any hon. member that this act be replaced-should not penalize either the farmers who live in the high risk areas or the people, including farmers, who live in a province that is a higher risk province than some others.
I believe it would be a good thing if the Minister of Agriculture would call into conference the representatives of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the representatives of the farmers union, the representatives of
Supply-Agriculture
the wheat pools and, if the government felt it was advisable, the representatives of the departments of agriculture of the various provinces in order to see how this present act could be expanded as to benefits and as to premiums and deductions so it could more nearly meet the heavy expenses that farmers incur when they have a crop failure.
As I have said, we feel that the benefits should be increased. We believe that if the benefits were substantially increased, agricultural producers would be prepared to have an increase made in the deductions at the elevator. This is an act that has the support of farm organizations and farmers generally. Any move the Minister of Agriculture may make to improve this act, either in respect of administration or in respect of the benefits that are paid thereunder, will receive the support of the people of the prairie provinces.

I should like to say a word or two in connection with the comments which have just been made, Mr. Chairman. First of all I should like to thank the hon. member for stating that his experience has been that the number of complaints in connection with this act have practically disappeared as a result of the amendments we brought in last year.
I did not say that.

I will say that. As a matter of fact the number of complaints we have had in my office this year has been almost negligible. I think you could count them on one hand. Last year and the year previous they came in literally by the hundreds and even by the thousands. I think that is the measure of the improvement made by last year's amendments with regard to removing causes for dissatisfaction on the part of the farmers in western Canada.
I do not think we should get into a discussion of crop insurance on this item. The hon. member started to talk about crop insurance but I am not going to do that. I should like to remind him and any other hon. members who may be wanting to talk about crop insurance that it was indicated in the speech from the throne that we were bringing in legislation on that subject this year. I think discussion of that matter should wait until that time, or at least until the general discussion on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, rather than be started here.
I might also say that this year it is estimated that payments from the emergency fund or in other words payments to farmers under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act will run to

Supply-Agriculture
better than $20 million. In other words an extensive program and extensive payments are in progress this year. I may also say that the payments made up to date are ahead of those made in any similar period in the last five years. Up to January 31, $8,447,725 had already been paid out. As to the remainder of the $20 million or a little better, the cheques are going out rapidly at the present time.

I have a small supplementary question. Can the minister refresh our memories as to the cost of prairie farm assistance as contemplated last summer when the crops looked bad? If my memory serves me correctly, and I am not saying that it does, I think the original estimate was that the cost might be as much as twice this amount.
The point I would like to make is this, that with the very substantial recovery of the prairie crop last summer even with the amendments of last year, which were in the direction of increasing the number of farmers who could obtain benefits, the amount of money which the government at one point anticipated would be necessary because the crop looked very bad was substantially reduced.

Mr. Chairman, if I may say so I think that is self apparent. If the crop improved the estimate of the amount we would have to put up would naturally be reduced. At one time we were estimating that payments would run between $30 million and $35 million, but now we estimate they will run to just about $20 million.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that this discussion would not be complete without some words from the constituency of Vegre-ville. Over the years we have had great difficulty with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act as it was. There was a great deal of dissatisfaction with the act as it was before the amendments were passed last year. In fact I owe that act a great debt of gratitude, because it was mainly on account of the difficulties experienced with the former prairies farm assistance act that I am here today. When I came down last session I had received some 400 separate complaints about the 1957 prairie farm assistance awards. Those were practically all looked after, to such an extent that a month ago I got payment for one section which had not been paid for in 1957. That was on account of an error in the office which was making out the various township maps. This year I have not had any more than a dozen complaints, and those complaints amounted more or less to inquiries.

There are still a few things that could be done to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to improve it, if it is to remain effective, and if it is not to be entirely superseded by crop insurance, which we may not discuss. One of the things that is not taken into account is the vagaries of rainfall and weather in our western country. It is an unfortunate thing that rain does not fall in square blocks. It does not fall in rectangular blocks, and it does not fall in blocks of twelve sections. It is, as I say, a very, very indeterminable and questionable area that lacks rainfall and consequently lacks crops. In my constituency there are areas of three or four sections which did not get rain, consequently they were not eligible under the act because they joined another block which got rain.
Just as an example, several years ago prairie farm assistance was paid in the area in which I farm. I had a very good crop. Bain fell on July 1 that just covered my farm. I produced 44 bushels of wheat to the acre that year, which even in the district in which I live is only part of a crop. I received through the Prairie Farm Assistance Act that year something in the amount of $300, because my neighbours did not get that rain. Now I would be cut out, as I have been ever since that time. But the main thing is that the act, as amended last year, has caused a great deal of satisfaction. It has caused prairie farm assistance to be distributed in a much more satisfactory manner, and consequently it is much more beneficial. Should this crop insurance plan for any reason not materialize, I certainly hope the Prairie Farm Assistance Act can be amended in the manner I have suggested. Then it would become almost a small crop insurance plan. I would have liked to say a few words about how much the $1 an acre bonus was appreciated, but I may not go into that.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words about these estimates. I have had a great deal of experience with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act brought in under the Liberal government but it never proved to be administered in a satisfactory way. They did not seem to take it seriously enough, or to amend the act so the farmers of western Canada would get proper payment under it. Last year western members spent a great deal of time in trying to amend this act, and I felt that we did a very good job in connection with it. I can quite appreciate the little speech today of the hon. member for Assiniboia, because he missed out and was not able to deal with those amendments-
Oh, no.
Well, if the hon. member will consult the record he will find that the amendments went through the house on that day.
I wonder if I might tell the hon. member that I was ill when these amendments were before the house, and that is why I missed them.

I would like to go back to February 3. Hon. members will remember that the hon. member for Assiniboia referred to us as a bunch of little mice. Well, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind you that those little mice had a big piece of cheese to nibble away at, and we were certainly getting the worms out of that act.
Were you nibbling at the worms?
No, they were not squirming enough for that. While these so-called mice were working on this act the Saskatchewan tom cat was running around the country howling.
Debate on a high level.

The hon. member for Assiniboia should give these little mice a great deal of credit for this act, because I am sure that his constituency will appreciate what we have done through these amendments. This act today is as much on an individual basis as it can possibly be.
I would like at this time to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture for the co-operation he has shown through the introduction of the amendments to this act, and I can assure you that there are several constituencies which have not had one complaint this year regarding the act as it stands today.
It did take a little more money for administration, but that was no fault of ours, because a great deal of inspection had to be carried out. I feel the expenditure of this extra sum of money was very necessary in order to carry out the provisions of this act.

I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture to give us a breakdown by provinces of the amount paid in levies by the farmers and the amounts received in prairie farm assistance payments since the inception of the act.

These figures are to be found in detail in the report of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act for the crop year 1957-58. The information is contained on the last two pages. This report is available to all hon. members, so I will not go into detail with regard to them. I will just give the total figures. From the inception of the act in 1939, and including the crop year 1957-58, the
Supply-Agriculture
amount of the 1 per cent levy collected in the three prairie provinces was as follows: Manitoba, $16 million; Saskatchewan, $60,800,000; Alberta, $30,426,000, making a total of $107,311,000. The payments out under the act to the three provinces for the same period were as follows: Manitoba, $13,943,000; Saskatchewan, $138,755,000; Alberta, $50,755,000. The total of these payments amounts to $204,353,000. There were some small payments in British Columbia which I have not included.

I ask this question because I should like to point out to hon. members that Manitoba is the only province which has received less than it has contributed. Our province is as you know, Mr. Chairman, known as the sure crop province. In round figures we paid in $16 million and we took out $13,900,000. Saskatchewan took out $138,700,000 and paid in $60 million; Alberta took out $50,700,000 where they had paid in $30 million.
I think it can be seen from these figures that the setting up of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has helped out the wheat area in Saskatchewan to a greater extent than it has assisted the other two provinces. I wanted to point this out because while it is possible that crop insurance would not work out in some areas, I believe it would work out very well in Manitoba where premiums would not be too high and where the payments received would be more in keeping with what was contributed.

I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture a question more for the sake of clarification than anything else. The minister has mentioned $20 million. May I ask if that sum is the amount paid out of the federal treasury to supplement the levy of 1 per cent?

That $20 million will consist of the 1 per cent levy collected plus the contribution from the consolidated revenue fund, that is from the dominion treasury. What the amount paid by the treasury will be this year we do not know, because grain deliveries have not all been made. However, the major portion of that payment of $20 million will come from the consolidated revenue fund. The complete breakdown, with regard to past years, is as I gave before; $204 million has been paid out and $107 million collected. In other words approximately half the money paid out from the beginning of the operation of the act up to the present time has come from general revenues and the other half has been collected by means of the 1 per cent levy.

Supply-Agriculture

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on this item I should first of all like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture on the hard work and effort he has put in, along with the rest of the western members, to amend this act. I think this work has been very satisfactory, and I gather from what has been said here today by hon. members that there have been very few complaints about the act as amended.
I should like, if I may, to comment on what was said by the hon. member for Assiniboia with regard to payments under P.F.A.A. The hon. member said, it will be recalled, that he would like to see up to $10 an acre paid on a 600-acre basis. This, I should say, would give up to $3,000 a year to a farmer with 600 acres, and I should like to go on record as stating that in my constituency-and I think I am correct in saying there is more P.F.A.A. assistance paid there than in any other constituency in Alberta- I have received no complaints whatever with regard to the maximum payment which has been decided on. I feel that if payments were made up to a limit of $3,000 it would have a very detrimental effect on the advancement of the agricultural industry, and that it would have a detrimental effect on farming in general and be harmful to the over-all efficiency of farming which today is the most important thing about farming.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, may I say a few words about this $225,000 increase in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I note that members from western Canada have been commending the government. I do not blame them. However, I should like to express the views of eastern farmers.
The member for Lisgar (Mr. Muir), who has just resumed his seat, suggested that Manitoba has not benefited from this legislation to the same extent as the others. I would point out that in the province of Quebec, it has not done us any good, because it does not apply. I realize that the act cannot now be amended for the benefit of eastern farmers. I would point out to the minister, however, that in the budget debate this item will come up, and we shall then have an opportunity to go into it more thoroughly. Nevertheless, I wish to say to the minister that eastern farmers are just as interested as western farmers in sharing the benefits of this legislation, which we endorse.
I have no objection to this increase, and if the minister will agree to consider the case of eastern farmers, he can count on

our help during the forthcoming debate on the budget. We shall then make known the needs of eastern farmers.
(Text):

It has been pointed out that I have advocated that the maximum payment under this act be increased from $4 to $10 an acre. Of course the $4 an acre payment is made only when the average yields are less than 3 bushels per acre, which in the general history of western Canada, as far as the total area is concerned, seldom happens. But in a year of catastrophe so far as the individual farmer is concerned, with a yield of 3 bushels an acre or less. I feel a payment of $10 an acre is not out of line. If the acreage on which this is paid were increased from 400 to 600 that naturally would bring a maximum payment of $3,000 in a year of total crop failure, and less in a period of partial crop failure of 3 to 5 bushels for the middle category or 5 to 8 bushels for the higher category.
Although I represent generally an agricultural riding I firmly believe that the Unemployment Insurance Act is an excellent piece of legislation and serves a useful purpose in Canada. Certainly we in this group shall be supporting increases in payments under that act. We have advocated this for many years. In fairness, and to keep things in perspective, it should be pointed out that payments are made at the rate of $33 a week, which on the basis of 52 weeks represents a payment of $1,760 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Order. This item is not for unemployment insurance.

Well, Mr. Chairman, prairie farm assistance if increased in the way I have suggested would bring some farmers in extraordinary years the sum of $3,000. It should be pointed out that this is not net income. Out of the $3,000 would have to be paid the very high costs of grain operations on a farm of maximum size. I would think that relative to the Unemployment Insurance Act my suggestion would bring prairie farm assistance somewhat in line with the benefits paid under that act. I want to make it crystal clear that what I have said should in no way be taken as a criticism of the benefits paid under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I believe that act should also be extended and improved.
I want to comment briefly on the statement that farmers in Manitoba have paid more into the act over the years than they have received out of it by way of benefits. That of course is perfectly true, and if one wished he could divide up the payments on the basis of municipalities or regions and make any kind of computation he desired. The operation of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is not based

on provincial boundaries but is designed to do a job for western Canada. One of the reasons the former minister of agriculture, Mr. Gardiner, used to vigorously advance the principle of this act, even though it provided frequently recurring payments in certain areas, was that the national agricultural policy of the federal government in years gone by settled people in the Palliser triangle, and once that was done the federal government had a responsibility to the producers in that area in times of crop failure. We in this group have always supported that principle as has, I believe, the present Minister of Agriculture.
In conversation with expert agriculturists from the prairie provinces I have discussed the possibility of having grain graded on the basis of protein content. The low yield areas over the years have generally experienced crops with a better protein content. The answer given to me was that farmers who produce the higher protein wheat are generally in the areas of crop failure and receive additional consideration under this act. Therefore, while it is true that certain farmers in specific regions have paid more into this act than they have obtained by way of benefits over the years, nevertheless as far as the value of wheat is concerned when the wheat is sold on the basis of protein content the situation is exactly reversed, and it has been suggested to me that some rough sort of justice obtains. As a result of the case being presented to me in this light I have been somewhat less active, shall I say, in championing the grading of wheat on the protein content basis, although I understand that active studies have been under way in recent years.
The point I wish to make is that the act was not drafted on the basis of provincial boundaries, and that federal governments in the past have taken the position that because national policy settled farmers in the Palliser triangle there was some responsibility on the part of the federal government and some is accepted in this act to protect the farmers' income during periods of crop failure.

Mr. Chairman, I feel I should remind the hon. member and other hon. members of the committee that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is not a crop insurance scheme, and it is therefore not correct to compare it to a system of crop insurance or to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The very name of the act indicates the function it fulfils. It was initially put into effect purely as a drought relief measure. Assistance under the act has also been extended to certain other forms of crop loss such as loss due to hail, flooding and grasshopper damage. Essentially this act remains a
Supply-C.B.C.
drought relief measure. It is not a system of crop insurance and it is futile to consider the principles underlying a system of crop insurance or the Unemployment Insurance Act in relation to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
I should also point out that the hon. member for Acadia was correct in stating that to increase payments to $10 an acre would not be wise. His riding is in one of the driest parts of Alberta, as is indicated by the fact that P.F.A.A. payments are always very extensive there whenever there is a year in which they are made.
I believe to increase the payments under the act to $10 an acre would result in a great deal of damage as far as conservation of the soil is concerned. To increase the payments would immediately cause a lot of land which should not be under the plough to be cultivated. Farmers would drill a crop into it and collect $10 an acre not caring whether or not they harvested anything. It would encourage poor methods of cultivation and other malpractices. To increase the payment would undoubtedly do a great deal of damage to our soil resources in western Canada. It would cause to be brought under cultivation land which should be left in grass, and this would be one of the most retrograde steps that could be taken.
Item agreed to.
700. Salaries and expenses of the board, $72,000.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a word or two about this item. This is not a large vote, but I notice it includes not only salaries for the new board but expenses as well, and I wonder if the minister would give us a breakdown of the amounts for salaries and expenses. I raise this question because I believe the new board has held its first public sittings within recent days.
People in the industry have indicated to me that they were rather surprised to find that the board is conducting its hearings with respect to applications in rather a new fashion, which I feel perhaps should be examined by the minister concerned. I am told that in the past when applications were heard by the C.B.C. board of governors it was most unusual to have questions from the board put through the voice of an official counsel, and similarly it was not usual for an applicant to feel obliged to attend with his solicitor.
I do not want to let down the profession of the Minister of Finance and myself. I can appreciate that a licensed station owner asked to appear before the board with respect to his public service conduct or some other

Supply-C.B.C.
breach of his obligations might wish to engage legal counsel. But when it is in connection with an application for a new licence I should think the public interest would be better served if the members of the board themselves did the questioning and heard directly from the actual person going to conduct the operation rather than listening to his counsel.
I simply draw that to the attention of the minister. The item refers to salaries and expenses, and I am wondering whether provision is being made for legal counsel, something that I believe was very rarely employed under the former procedure.
With respect to engineering and professional advice concerning electronics and other technical matters, upon whom will the new board rely? Will they rely solely on the officials of the Department of Transport or will they be relying, as the former board did, upon advice from the engineering people in the C.B.C., or will the board be hiring new technical and professional people to assist them in matters of this kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the item under discussion, No. 700, is to provide for the salaries and expenses of the members of the board from November 20, 1958, to March 31 next, the end of the fiscal year. It covers the salaries of the full-time members of the board, of whom there are three, and in the case of the other members of the board their per diem allowances and travelling and other expenses in attending meetings.
So far as salaries are concerned, the appropriation is to provide for the salaries of 13 members of the staff subject always, of course, to the approval of the establishment by treasury board. The item also covers such things as supplies, equipment and office rental.
My hon. friend asked questions about the method of conducting the hearings and about the use of technical advisers. So far as the method of conducting hearings is concerned, I think that is a matter for the board itself to determine in the light of its responsibilities. I understand some view was expressed that in the case of applicants the board wished in some cases to hear directly from the applicant, but I have no reason to think there is any wish on the part of the board to tell applicants that they should not seek the services of counsel if they choose to do so.
It is the other way around. I think the board itself has set a new pattern in conducting the questioning through counsel rather than the board doing so directly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I would rather be allowed to continue my remarks in the manner in which I had intended to make them. If I should be out of order the chairman will call me to order, but I shall do my utmost to stick to the item before the committee.

As I said earlier, the parties to the dispute are now negotiating their differences and that is all to the good. I commend those who are responsible for bringing these people together. So far as we on this side of the house are concerned, they have our very best wishes that they will be able to bring the dispute to a satisfactory conclusion as quickly as possible. No one will be happier than I if such is the case, because I am sure that no one, whether on this side of the house or on the other side, is anxious to see any group of individuals suffer because of a difficulty such as the one which has arisen.
But in dealing with this matter objectively it strikes me that there are some things that the minister responsible for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its operations should take into account. There are the long term and short term effects of any dispute, whether this one or another one that may take place involving the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its producers or other employees. Of course, as I said a moment ago, it is unfortunate that 1,300 people, together with the producers, should have been out of work for almost 39 days. However, that is something which has taken place and there is nothing that can be done about it at the moment save and except to continue the efforts that are being made at present to bring about conciliation of the dispute.
But because of the nature of the operations of the corporation there are long term effects of such a dispute and the long term effects I have in mind relate to the future of the French network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I am sure I do not have to convince you, Mr. Chairman, that the group of people who are responsible for having established the French network have done a magnificent job. If tribute is to be given to the C.B.C. by all means let them have it, but credit must be given to these producers who are responsible in no small measure for creating the interest they have thus far in the kind of programs that have been seen on the French television network.
I am not an artist, and I do not pretend to know what are the exigencies of the technical side of the programs. I believe, however, I can appreciate whether or not a program is good. I have been told and retold that these producers not only compare with their brothers in the rest of Canada but are far superior to those in Paris. The productions they have been staging on the French network are, in fact, far superior to the programs which are produced in Paris.
Now, that is going quite a long way. This information comes to me from very reliable sources. Those of us who have watched the
Supply-C.B.C.
programs can well believe that is the case. Well, if it is the case, as I have every reason to believe it is, then I think the greatest care should be taken in the future, as at the present time, to see that the talent of those producers is not lost and that its benefits are given to Canada.
Dealing still with the operations of the C.B.C., there is one thing which I think has been entirely forgotten in so far as this dispute is concerned, and that is that it is not regional; it is not a local matter. It is a national matter. It is of national importance that there should be adequate service for the French television network. It is a matter, I am sure, of importance to the English speaking Canadians who are interested in bicultural Canadianism for Canada that the best possible kind of programs be available for the French network.
Having said that, I am sure the house will accept what I am saying in the spirit in which it is given, namely that here is a group of people who have done their utmost to bring about productions which are second to none in their field, and that every effort should be made to bring about a settlement of this unfortunate dispute at the earliest possible moment. I say again that I welcome the efforts that have been made thus far to bring this matter to a successful conclusion. I trust and hope that those who are responsible for having brought the parties together will be successful in their endeavours to negotiate a satisfactory settlement of this dispute.

years the speediest expansion of T.V. services of all countries of the world.

million, in spite of the money it had received from the treasury and of the considerable amounts it had drawn.

I should like to deal with the subject which has been dealt with by the hon. member for Laurier, though I intend to deal with a slightly different aspect of this problem. Before I commence my remarks on that subject, I should like to make a comment on the remarks made by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm. He has pointed out what he deems to be the extravagance of the Canadian people in supporting the C.B.C. I want to point out that the Canadian people do not support only the C.B.C., but in addition they support all the private radio and television stations across this country. The money to cover the cost of these stations comes from the people of Canada and from no one else, whether it comes as a few cents on your tax bill at the end of the year or whether it comes as an extra 5 cents on your cake of soap. I think our contribution toward the C.B.C. is one which is worth while for the Canadian people. In this way the Canadian government will at least have something to say about the programs that are presented to the Canadian people and prevent the C.B.C. being sold to Lux soap or some other such organization.
What concerns me about this particular estimate with which we are dealing, which

is to cover the anticipated deficit of the C.B.C. this year, is that a portion of this anticipated deficit will have gone to fight this particular strike we have now.

speechtext: Does my hon. friend wish me to clear up that point now?
At the conclusion of my remarks.

speechtext: It has nothing to do with it.

I have here a copy of a pamphlet which runs to 13 pages and which is entitled "The History of the Dispute between Montreal television producers association and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation". This pamphlet sets out the management's side of the problem. I do not know who produced it or where it was produced, but I assume that it was produced on C.B.C. time, that C.B.C. material was used, and so forth. I have also seen copies of the telegrams sent to the wives of the employees involved in the strike at Montreal. The cost of these must have run into a considerable sum.
It is unfortunate that we have a dispute such as we have now in Montreal, but the fact still remains that if we do have a fight it should be a fair one. One of the major complaints that has been brought to my attention by both the producers and the others who have supported them so strongly is that the C.B.C. has been given an opportunity of presenting its side of the case while the others have had to use whatever means were available to them. Let us remember that the C.B.C. costs are paid by the Canadian government and the money is raised by the Canadian people. Here we have a case in which something for which the Canadian people as a whole pay is being used by one side in a particular dispute. I feel that is something that should be given very careful consideration. The government are responsible for this matter. If things like this must happen, they should ensure that it should be fair for all the people concerned. It should be fair for the people who are now on strike and for the people who support that strike. They have just as big a stake in it as anyone else.
We have had many references to the legality and illegality of this thing. We find that our cabinet, along with many other people in Canada, cannot make up their minds as to the legal or the illegal aspects. I do not think the legality or illegality of the strike is really the most important aspect of this matter. We can remember the time a few years ago when child labour was legal in mines and so on in this and other countries. Today it is unheard of. It is not only illegal

today but it is also unthinkable. Laws change from time to time. I think the most important thing for this government to find out is not necessarily whether it is legal or illegal but whether it is right, just and fair. We may find things which are legal but which are not fair or just. That is the time when we change the laws in order to ensure that what is fair and just is legal as well.
We had one illustration of this sort of thing by the Minister of National Revenue in the house, I believe just last week. He gave the house the impression, which possibly he innocently had himself, that the picketers had been responsible for certain acts of violence. But the following day, on being questioned in the house, he admitted that he was not sure and that nobody knew just who was responsible for this thing. That is one illustration of the point I have been making. I think this government owes a deep responsibility, in connection with these disputes which arise in government departments, to let us know exactly or at least as closely as we can possibly find out who is right and who is wrong before we take any position or make any statements.
There is something else that all hon. members in this house should realize and look closely into, namely the situation itself. I am speaking particularly to the English speaking members representing English speaking areas of Canada. I do not think they have realized just how important and vital this matter is. I heard a newspaper reporter the other day discussing this situation. He brought out an extremely important point. He said that for English speaking Canadians to get a true and proper conception of this particular situation it would be necessary for us to have a situation in which Wayne and Shuster, Juliette and all the other top television stars in Canada as well as the top television stars in the United States which are carried on the English network in Canada, such as Ed Sullivan, Perry Como, and so on would be out on the picket line. He said that if they were out on the picket line it would mean exactly the same thing to English speaking Canadians as does the present situation to French speaking Canadians throughout Canada. I think that is something we have completely overlooked, namely the national importance of this dispute that has been going on.
I believe the government should have gone into it much sooner than they did. I should also like to convey my congratulations to whoever has been responsible for getting the parties together. That is the only way in which this dispute can ever be settled. As long as they are apart there will be no settlement. I also think this government owes a
Supply-C.B.C.
duty to make sure, first of all, what is right and what is wrong and then, if necessary, to have the necessary laws passed so that whatever is right may also be legal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Before any other hon. members speak under any misapprehension as to the reason this item comes before the house, Mr. Chairman, I think I should give a brief explanation with regard to it. As hon. members will recall, one of the sources of the revenues of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for some years has been the revenue yielded by the excise tax on receiving sets and tubes. When the operating budget of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was drawn up for the present fiscal year, namely 1958-59, it of course was based on the assumption that $12 million would be received from that excise tax which was earmarked for the sustenance of the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. When the new broadcasting act was proclaimed in November, further receipts from the excise tax were cancelled. That was the effect of the act. Of the $12 million that had been provided in the estimates for 1958-59, the corporation had received $9,806,448. Consequently the present item of $2,193,552 is simply the amount remaining out of the original $12 million which was the anticipated yield from that excise tax.
The vote for this sum now becomes necessary to meet the operating requirements of the corporation to the end of the present fiscal year. It does not therefore represent, in the net result, any increase at all in the amount required to conduct the national broadcasting system of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. In a sense it is a revote, but it arises simply in the manner I have indicated, namely because of the repeal of what was a statutory provision directing that the yield from the excise tax should go automatically to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, no additional vote whatever is involved here. Not an additional cent of taxpayers' money is being appropriated by this item to the support of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation at all.
In fact it is a subtraction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is simply in effect a revote.

Mr. Chairman, while we
are on this item, I feel it is my duty

Supply-C.B.C.
to add a few words to what has already been said, in view of the current dispute between the C.B.C. and Montreal radio and T.V. producers. I am sure we all deplore that strike, and hope it will be settled just as soon as possible. However, I regret to note that among those who are attempting to settle the dispute, some are more or less active, or perhaps should I say more or less inactive, in achieving this purpose.
I do not believe that we, who are sitting on the side of the opposition, are open to criticism in this regard. Indeed, even some members on the government side thought it proper at the last minute to step in and work towards the settlement of the dispute. They have done so, no doubt after noting the inaction or confusion of the government which, I am convinced, would like the dispute to be settled but which, unfortunately and in my humble opinion, has failed to take the proper means of doing so.
Mr. Chairman, as stated this morning by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin), this is a national problem, a national emergency, affecting at least a third of our population.
I was reading in the papers, last week, that there are roughly 3 million T.V. sets in Canada, and I think I can safely say that a third of them are in French-Canadian homes. On the basis of an average of three or four listeners per home, it means that nearly four million French Canadians are affected by this strike, and would like to see it settled, because they are taxpayers, especially since the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) has mentioned that the province of Quebec is like any other province.
We all remember the railway strike that took place at the time when Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent was prime minister. Mr. St. Laurent had described it as a national emergency in the economic field. My feeling is that the present dispute is likewise a national emergency in the cultural field. As a matter of fact, I wonder what the hon. members who speak the other official language would think if, instead of a French network producers' strike, there was a strike on the English network.
The hon. member for Timmins referred to fine programs: Perry Como's, Ed. Sullivan's and others. The French-Canadian population also enjoys fine programs such as The Plouffe Family and others. It also likes to get the T.V. news, to hear talks and to watch such programs as Point de mire, Un homme et son peche, etc.
And Seraphin!

Mr. Chairman, I think Seraphin would be a typical example of the present government. As a matter of fact, I would even say that the present government is behaving very much like Seraphin, in regard to the settlement of this emergency. We know that our friends opposite are always eager for suggestions. They want to run the country, but only in so far as we make suggestions to them.
One suggestion I can offer to the government as a means of settling this strike is to follow the example of the former prime minister, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, who settled the railway strike to the satisfaction of all Canadians. That strike was that of an independent, autonomous corporation. But as it created an emergency affecting the majority of Canadians, as soon as the prime minister heard that a dispute was imminent, he wrote a letter to the parties involved, asking them to reach some agreement and showing the advantages and disadvantages of a possible strike. When the strike loomed closer and closer, the government offered to appoint a mediator, a suggestion which was accepted by the parties. Both sides then attempted until the last minute to reach a settlement. But when all its attempts at conciliation had failed, and when it realized that the strike was inevitable, the Liberal government of that time, conscious, as any government should be, of its responsibilities, called a session of parliament to put an end to this economic crisis.
Now what has the present government done so far? Since the house is now in session, there is no need to call a special session of Parliament. If the members of the cabinet, and hon. members opposite, had only studied the pros and cons of the dispute, they would have read the opinions of experts in such matters, such as Father Jacques Cousineau, S.J., a professor in the law faculty of the University of Montreal; Father Gerard Dion, director of industrial relations of Laval University; and Mr. Jean Rheal Cardin, director of industrial relations at the University of Montreal. They would have found that, in the opinion of those three experts, the only way to reach a settlement of this dispute is through arbitration.
I suggest that, to solve this national dispute, the government follow the procedure that was established at the very beginning

of the second 1950 session. I call it national because it affects a third of the population in the cultural field, and because the people involved in it run into the millions. 1 would also point out that the C.B.C., in addition to operating in the red at the present time, is losing money through failure to carry out its contracts with sponsors or advertisers. It should also be remembered that those who dare not or will not cross the picket lines are now out of work, and therefore are getting no pay and do not qualify for unemployment insurance.
Mr. Chairman, I hope this dispute will be settled as soon as possible, and I commend the parties who are now striving to reach an immediate settlement. I feel the government should consider the matter more fully than it has done so far, notwithstanding the claims of the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer), and I urge the Minister of National Revenue to take advantage of the help offered by the Solicitor General if need be, or by any of their own members who, being faced as we are by the government's failure to act, have decided to do something on their own.

Mr. Chairman, I would at once follow in the footsteps of my hon. friend, the member for St. Denis, who spoke very forcefully about the circumstances as we find them now. However, the house will excuse me if I turn to another aspect of this question, and it is one with which I am sure the minister is familiar. The item under discussion deals, of course, with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the operating deficit, and the point I should like to make at the moment has to do with the present membership of the executive committee of the board of directors of the C.B.C. which was ultimately responsible for the action taken by the corporation in this unfortunate dispute.
When the new Broadcasting Act was discussed in this house not so long ago-I believe it was in August of last year-we on this side of the house intimated to the government that very careful consideration should be given to the qualifications of members of the two boards because if this were not done serious difficulties might arise in the future. Perhaps I might be allowed to put on record the question which was asked by the Leader of the Opposition and the reply which was given by the Minister of National Revenue. The question is taken from Hansard of August 25, at page 4097: 66968-9-49

Would anybody who owned shares in a press association or chain of newspapers also be disqualified by ownership of shares in that press chain from sitting on this board if that press chain or corporation also ran a broadcasting station?

I am not prepared to give a legal opinion on such a set of facts. As my hon. friend knows, every set of facts varies slightly one from another. All lawyers know that. I think a person would be very reckless to attempt to give a legal opinion today which would be of no avail anyway because if this matter were dealt with administratively it would have to be dealt with by justice and if it went further it would have to be dealt with by the courts. But I would suggest to the Leader of the Opposition that the words "directly or indirectly, as owner, shareholder, director, officer, partner, or otherwise" are very broad and will preclude many people from taking a position on the board. There can be no question about that; I do not want to try to give a legal definition of the area as to who is going to be excluded and who is going to be included.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate interjected at this point to say this:
But either the minister or some other minister or the Prime Minister is going to have to recommend certain names to the governor in council and the governor in council is going to have to appoint these people. Therefore it does seem to me that since parliament is being asked to make this enactment we should know precisely what this provision is supposed to mean. Would, for example, a shareholder in Canadian General Electric, which probably makes and sells parts of radio apparatus, be excluded or would somebody owning shares in Canadian Investment Fund, which might happen in turn to own some shares in Canadian General Electric, be thereby excluded? It seems to me that this is very vague and very far-reaching indeed and that perhaps it would be worth while to take another look at it for it might turn out that about the only people who will be eligible in the country will be farmers, fishermen and the unemployed.
I want to put on record one other quotation from the hon. member for Ottawa West, who made the following observation:
What about people engaged in the distribution of radio apparatus? Chain stores distribute radio apparatus. Would this apply to employees of chain stores?
The matter which I seek to bring to the attention of the minister in the house is that at that time, in the course of the debate we on this side warned the government of the danger of not taking extreme care as to who might or might not be appointed and sworn in as members of the board of directors. We gave a warning having to do with the composition of these two boards, and now we have good reason to believe that at least one member of the board of directors of the C.B.C.-there may be others-does not meet the qualifications set out in section 22, paragraph 6. I should

Supply-C.B.C.
like to read the appropriate part of section 22, which reads as follows:
Every director shall, before entering upon his duties as such, take and subscribe, before the Clerk of the Privy Council, an oath in the following form:
I do solemnly swear that I will faithfully, truly and impartially, to the best of my judgment, skill and ability execute and perform the office of director of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and that, while I continue to hold such office, I will not, as owner, shareholder, director, officer, partner or otherwise, engage in the business of broadcasting or have any pecuniary or proprietary interest in a broadcasting station or in the manufacture or distribution of radio apparatus.
I should like to draw the attention of the minister to the last words, "distribution of radio apparatus". If we go back to the Radio Act, which I have before me here, we see that in section 2, subsection 1, there is a definition of radio apparatus which reads as follows:
Radio apparatus means a reasonably complete and sufficient combination of distinct radio appliances intended for or capable of being used for radio electric communication whether for transmission or reception or both.
On the other hand, the word "distribution" as opposed to manufacture covers all levels of distribution, that is, retail as well as wholesale. Although I am told there is no formal definition of the word "distribution" in our statutes, that is the meaning which is generally accepted in practice. It is the definition which is applied, for example, by the combines investigation branch of the Department of Justice and by the restrictive trade practices commission. That commission has published several reports dealing with this: subject. For instance, there is a report in my hand-and I quote-"concerning an alleged combine in the distribution and sale of gasoline at retail in the Vancouver area." This clearly indicates that distribution covers retailing, and this can only mean that anyone who is engaged in selling radio reception sets is not eligible to either of the broadcasting boards. However, my information is to the effect that one of the members of the board, who happens to be Mr. Raymond Dupuis of Montreal, is still president of Dupuis et Freres which is a large department store selling radio and television sets.
In spite of this, he was sworn in as a member of the board of directors of the C.B.C. on December 4, and at a meeting of that board in Montreal later on he was elected to be a member of the executive committee. Moreover, I am informed he was the only French speaking member of that committee from the province of Quebec to attend the meetings during the dispute, though he was not entitled to sit in that capacity.
[Mr. Chevrier.l
In order that there may be no misunderstanding of my position, I want to make clear that as far as Mr. Raymond Dupuis himself is concerned I consider him as a friend of mine. I know him. He is a man of distinction and a man highly respected in Montreal business circles. He is not only successful but is known throughout Canada, and I would not want anything that I am saying here to be interpreted as impugning or attacking his personal character or reputation in any way whatsoever. What I am doing, and what I maintain I have a perfect right to do if the circumstances are as I have related them, is this: I submit that this matter has been badly handled, and I maintain that the government has been badly advised in inviting a person who is in this position to become a member of the board of directors.
I say this because we on this side of the house warned the government about the position last year. We warned the government with regard to this aspect of the legislation, as I have already made clear, and if the facts as I have related them are correct, this gentleman, estimable as he may be, has been placed in a highly irregular situation by the government and I think the government, through the minister responsible for the C.B.C., owes an explanation to the house with reference to this matter. I think he should take the first opportunity to report to the house whether or not these facts are correct. If they are not correct, then, of course, I shall desist immediately. I believe the minister should also report whether the executive committee of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation would have taken an attitude different from that they have taken up until the time the negotiations were resumed with respect to the dispute if Mr. Dupuis had not been attending the meetings.
It seems to me that the government through the minister must make a clear and full statement about this matter because it could throw a new light on the position of the C.B.C. in regard to the dispute. I am sure the minister would understand that in raising the point I do so in a constructive rather than a destructive way because, if the facts as I have related them are so, then the situation is serious.
